Day 62 of 100 · Docker

Docker Architecture

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityDockerPublished artifact recovered

Docker is a client-server system: the CLI sends API requests, the daemon manages Docker objects and registries distribute images.

Architecture / mental model

Docker CLI → Docker API/socket → dockerd → container runtime / images / networks / volumes
                                ↕
                              registry

How it works

The `docker` command is the client. It parses instructions such as `docker run`, `docker ps` and `docker build` and sends API requests rather than creating containers itself.

`dockerd` is the persistent daemon that manages images, containers, networks and volumes and coordinates lower-level runtime operations.

Registries store and distribute images. When `docker run nginx` needs an image that is not available locally, the daemon can pull it from the configured registry before creating and starting the container.

Hands-on reference

docker version
docker info
sudo systemctl status docker
ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

Verification

Use `docker version` to distinguish client and server information, then stop or inspect the daemon in a safe lab and observe how client-side information can still appear before a daemon connection failure.

Field note / gotcha

Access to `/var/run/docker.sock` is effectively privileged. Members of the `docker` group can control the daemon and commonly gain root-equivalent host capabilities.

Security considerations

Do not expose an unauthenticated Docker API on the network. Protect remote daemon access with SSH or TLS and tightly control socket/group membership.

What I learned

When Docker fails, identify whether the client, daemon, image/registry, runtime or host layer failed instead of blaming one mysterious box called Docker.
